title: Holy War and the Ban
lead: Wars that the Bible says God commanded, some under the herem, the "ban" that devoted a city or people to destruction (Deuteronomy 7; 20; Joshua 6; 1 Samuel 15; Numbers 31). These texts are among the hardest in Scripture, and Jews and Christians have read them in sharply different ways: as unique judgments, as ancient war language not meant to be repeated, or as violence to be read critically.

sections.b: Israel's wars are called "the wars of the LORD" (Numbers 21:14; 1 Samuel 18:17). The herem ban meant giving a conquered city wholly to God, by destroying it, its people and often its goods (Deuteronomy 7:1–2; 20:16–18; Joshua 6:17–21). Distant cities were to be offered peace first (Deuteronomy 20:10–15). Similar language appears outside the Bible: the Moabite king Mesha boasts that he devoted the Israelite town of Nebo to his god Chemosh and killed its people.

Some traditional readers defend the commands as God's just judgment on peoples whose sin had reached its full measure, as Genesis 15:16 foresees ("the guilt of the Amorites is not yet full"), limited to that time and place. Others note that the same books say the Canaanites were "driven out" rather than wiped out, and read the ban language as war rhetoric like that of other ancient nations. The rabbis limited the commands to the seven nations of Canaan and Amalek. Later they held that those peoples can no longer be identified, applying the Mishnah's principle that Sennacherib mixed up the nations (Mishnah Yadayim 4:4, about an Ammonite convert) to the seven nations as well (Bavli Berakhot 28a; Maimonides). Many modern scholars treat the texts as ideology to be read critically. The New Testament's call to love enemies (Matthew 5:43–48) has led most Christians to read them as part of a story that does not license war today.
